title: What is Stream.mapMulti (Java 16): it pushes 0..N elements to a Consumer instead of returning a sub-stream like flatMap: when is it more efficient, and how do you use it?
shortTitle: Stream.mapMulti (Java 16): push 0..N elements imperatively, vs flatMap
keyPoints: mapMulti pushes elements to a downstream Consumer imperatively instead of creating a Stream per element
More efficient than flatMap when producing 0 or 1 element per input (no Stream.of/empty overhead)
Useful for imperative logic: loops, conditions, multiple conditional outputs
Primitive variants: mapMultiToInt, mapMultiToLong, mapMultiToDouble avoid boxing
Java 16+ via JEP (added as API enhancement, no separate JEP number)
Use flatMap when the mapping naturally produces a Stream (Collection::stream)
Use mapMulti when the mapping is conditional or involves imperative loops

s1_definition.oneliner: Stream.mapMulti pushes 0 to N elements to a Consumer imperatively instead of creating a Stream per element like flatMap, avoiding per-element stream allocation overhead.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Signature** – `mapMulti(BiConsumer<T, Consumer<R>>)`: for each input element, push zero, one, or many output elements to the downstream Consumer.
- **vs flatMap** – flatMap allocates a Stream object per element (even for 0 or 1 output). mapMulti calls `consumer.accept()` directly.
- **Best for** – conditional emission (0 or 1 element per input), imperative loops, and type casting.
- **Primitive variants** – `mapMultiToInt`, `mapMultiToLong`, `mapMultiToDouble` avoid boxing.
s1_definition.analogy: flatMap: each clerk creates a tray of items and puts the tray on the belt. mapMulti: each clerk places items directly on the belt one by one. For one or zero items per clerk, skipping the tray saves work.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  flatMap vs mapMulti:

  flatMap: element → Stream → flatten
    Trade(split) → Stream(leg1, leg2) → leg1, leg2
    Trade(normal) → Stream.of(trade) → trade
    Per-element Stream allocation!

  mapMulti: element → push to Consumer
    Trade(split) → accept(leg1), accept(leg2)
    Trade(normal) → accept(trade)
    Zero Stream allocation!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Stream.mapMulti (Java 16) pushes elements to a Consumer imperatively instead of returning a Stream like flatMap. It is more efficient for conditional emission (0 or 1 element per input) because flatMap allocates a Stream object per element even for single-element output. mapMulti just calls `consumer.accept()` directly.

Use flatMap when the mapping naturally produces a Stream (Collection::stream). Use mapMulti when the mapping is conditional, involves imperative loops, or mostly produces 0 or 1 element. Primitive variants (mapMultiToInt, mapMultiToLong, mapMultiToDouble) avoid boxing.

Remember one sentence: mapMulti pushes elements imperatively to a Consumer, avoiding the per-element Stream allocation that flatMap creates.
